title: Tools vs Technique: The Capability Gap
author: Anthea Roberts

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that value depends on workflow redesign, verification judgement and organisational capability rather than tool access alone. It materially extends that proposition with a small-team adoption case showing that capability develops unevenly even with access and training, and with a concrete prescription for sustained, applied and supported practice.
qs: The bottleneck is the human and organisational capacity to use the tools.
Nearly everyone had an "ah ha" moment — but it required sustained, applied, supported practice.

kp.k: Foundational adoption differs from augmenting complex knowledge work
kp.d: Roberts distinguishes Level 1 adoption—governance, security, infrastructure and routine-task automation—from Level 2, which augments analysis, synthesis and judgement through structured agents, skills, workflows and context. She argues that foundational work is becoming table stakes, while differentiated organisational value requires orchestration of AI for harder work. This is a cross-domain organisational framework, not a legal-sector finding.
qs: Level 1 automates the routine. Level 2 augments the hard stuff — the analysis, the synthesis, the judgement calls.
It requires knowing how to build systems that structure how AI reasons through problems — agents, skills, workflows, context — and the judgement to orchestrate them.

kp.k: Technique, rather than tool access, constrains realised capability
kp.d: Roberts argues that people using identical tools obtain different results because of differences in workflow redesign, practical fluency, understanding model limitations and building accessible context. She asserts that almost nobody has crossed from Level 1 to Level 2 and that the gap is widening as models improve faster than human technique; these are authorial claims rather than quantified research findings.
qs: Two people can sit down with exactly the same AI tool and get wildly different results.
The gap between those two people is not a tools gap. It is a technique gap.
The models improve exponentially. Human technique improves linearly or in step changes.

kp.k: AI-native practice contrasts sharply with enterprise adoption
kp.d: Roberts reports that her small AI-native firm has rebuilt essentially every workflow around human–AI collaboration, with each team member running thirty or more AI sessions a day and using voice dictation with coding agents. She contrasts this first-person experience with conversations at government agencies and major corporations still navigating Copilot adoption or considering alternatives. The comparison is experiential rather than a systematic enterprise survey.
qs: I run a small AI-native firm where my team and I talk to coding agents through voice dictation, run thirty or more AI sessions a day each, and have rebuilt essentially every workflow we have around human-AI collaboration.

I also spend my weeks talking to large organisations — government agencies, major corporations — where smart, capable people are still trying to figure out how to use Copilot or whether to venture beyond it.

kp.k: Practical AI fluency requires immersion, not short training
kp.d: Roberts characterises Level 2 technique as metis: embodied practical intelligence acquired through sustained applied work. She argues that this know-how currently resides almost entirely in AI-native startups whose teams can repeatedly rebuild, fail and iterate. Manuals, two-day workshops and six-week scoped pilots cannot substitute for immersion, although working alongside experienced practitioners can help.
qs: The technique — the embodied know-how of working with AI at Level 2 — currently resides almost entirely in AI-native startups.
You can't acquire it in a two-day workshop. You can't get it from a pilot programme that runs for six weeks with a carefully scoped use case.
Metis comes from doing. From immersion. From time in the water.

kp.k: Tool-using agents demand redesigned workflows and checking judgements
kp.d: Roberts describes moving from extensive chatbot use to Claude Code as a shift to a collaborator capable of multi-round reasoning, searches, document retrieval and local file editing. These capabilities also introduced risks, including deletion of important files. She reports spending months learning what to trust and check, rebuilding filing systems for agent readability, and deciding when to direct the agent versus letting it reason.
qs: It could reason over multiple rounds with searches and tool calls rather than replying straight away.
If I wasn't careful, it could also delete important files on my computer (note: ask me how I know this)!

I had to learn what to trust Claude Code with and what to check. I had to rebuild my filing systems so agents could read them. I had to develop judgement about when to direct and when to let it reason. That took months, not days.

kp.k: Access and initial training did not ensure team adoption
kp.d: Within a willing team of fewer than ten people, Roberts reports that access, initial training and multiple weekly drop-in sessions did not spread technique automatically. She subsequently mandated agent use and provided hands-on support. Some adopted quickly and others needed weeks; nearly everyone eventually had an insight into its value. Her account supports sustained, applied, supported practice and personally engaged leadership, but is a single-team experience.
qs: We gave everyone access and initial training followed by multiple drop-in sessions a week for people to get help on how to connect various things and improve their techniques.
When encouragement didn't work for everyone, I eventually mandated the use of these agents.
Some converted quickly. Others needed weeks. Nearly everyone had an "ah ha" moment — but it required sustained, applied, supported practice.
And that's a team of fewer than ten people who already wanted to be there.

kp.k: Enterprise constraints create a structural capability mismatch
kp.d: Roberts argues that large organisations managing billions and making decisions affecting millions have particularly urgent capability needs but face greater obstacles to developing AI-native fluency. Governance obligations, fiduciary duties, legacy systems, regulatory constraints and workforce-scale change limit their freedom to reconstruct workflows, unlike startups where she locates the relevant know-how.
qs: They have governance obligations, fiduciary duties, legacy systems, regulatory constraints, hundreds of employees who all need to be brought along.
The know-how resides in startups — small teams who have had the freedom to rebuild everything.
But the urgent need for that know-how sits inside enterprises that can't rebuild anything without a business case, a risk assessment, and a change management plan.

kp.k: Capability transfer may bridge software and organisational practice
kp.d: Roberts proposes capability transfer through embedded collaboration, agent and workflow starter packs, and applied work on real problems, rather than software procurement alone. She explicitly leaves the institutional model unresolved, asking whether enterprises will acquire startups for their people and practices or adopt arrangements unlike conventional consulting or software. She reports seeing acqui-hires over the last year in Silicon Valley and growing mixed software–service offerings, including forward-deployed engineers and consultancies with software capabilities, without presenting systematic evidence.
qs: You can't buy technique. You can't subscribe to metis. You have to develop it yourself even if it makes an enormous difference to have people working alongside you to show you the way.

The actual know-how of working with AI at the level that changes what's possible, transferred through embedding with teams, building together based on agent and workflow starter packs, and learning through applied work on real problems.
I genuinely don't know what the bridge looks like yet.
We are increasingly seeing mixed software and service offerings, whether it is software firms with forward-deployed engineers or consulting firms with software capabilities.

kp.k: Organisational learning capacity will determine AI value capture
kp.d: Roberts concludes that strong outcomes require tools, techniques and curated organisational context together. She shifts the strategic question from model selection to who can learn rapidly and how practical knowledge can move between groups without organisational reinvention. Her claim that human and organisational capability will determine who captures technological value is a forward-looking judgement.
qs: Really good outcomes in AI come from combining the best tools with the best techniques and applying them to your own curated context.
The bottleneck is the human and organisational capacity to use the tools.
And that bottleneck is going to define who actually captures the value of this technology — and who just talks about it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Roberts argues that the principal constraint on AI-driven organisational value is practical human and organisational capability, rather than access to tools. This is a cross-domain argument about complex knowledge work, not a specific claim about legal services.
pts.d: Roberts distinguishes Level 1 adoption—governance foundations and routine automation—from Level 2, which augments analysis, synthesis and judgement through agents, workflows, skills and curated context. She claims that almost nobody has crossed to Level 2 and that differences in technique explain markedly different results from identical tools. She further claims that the capability gap is widening because model improvements outpace human learning. Her framing emphasises human-AI collaboration and orchestration, not autonomous replacement of professionals.

pts.k: Roberts claims that agentic AI changes work from prompting a chatbot to co-creating with a system that can act on files and use tools, requiring redesigned workflows and judgement about supervision.
pts.d: Her account of Claude Code attributes the change to combining model reasoning with a tool-enabled harness: document retrieval and storage, multi-round reasoning, searches, and file editing. She reports that this required reorganising filing systems for agent access and learning what to trust, what to check, and when to direct the agent. The ability to act also creates risks, illustrated by her reference to deletion of important files. She presents practical fluency as knowledge acquired through sustained applied work, rather than short training or access alone.

pts.k: Roberts identifies a mismatch between AI-native startups holding practical know-how and large enterprises needing it, and proposes capability transfer rather than software procurement alone.
pts.d: She claims that Level 2 know-how currently resides almost entirely in small AI-native startups able to rebuild workflows, whereas enterprises face governance, fiduciary, regulatory, legacy-system and workforce constraints. She proposes embedded collaboration, agent and workflow starter packs, and learning on real problems as ways to transfer capability. She treats acquisitions for people and practices and hybrid software-service models as possible bridges, explicitly leaving the eventual model unresolved. Her proposal is not that software is unnecessary, but that tools must be combined with technique and organisation-specific context.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily Roberts's first-person experience of an AI-native team and conversations with large organisations, supplemented by general observations of market activity.
pts.d: Roberts reports running a team of fewer than ten, using thirty or more AI sessions per person daily, rebuilding workflows, and spending months learning agentic work despite substantial prior chatbot experience. Her internal adoption account describes initial training, repeated support sessions, mandated agent use, and differing learning speeds. These provide experiential support for her claims about the difficulty of spreading technique. She also cites conversations with government agencies and major corporations, and points to Silicon Valley acqui-hires and mixed software-service offerings without naming cases or providing outcome data. No systematic adoption survey, benchmark, controlled comparison, or quantified productivity or financial result is supplied for the broader claims about near-universal Level 1 adoption, the concentration of know-how, or the widening capability gap. Sarah Guo's quoted post introduces the contrast, but the substantive argument is Roberts's own.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The diagnosis concerns the state of adoption in March 2026; learning is described as taking weeks or months, while the prediction about value capture has no specified deadline.
pts.d: Writing on 16 March 2026, Roberts describes foundations as becoming table stakes and the capability gap as widening monthly. Her own transition to agentic collaboration took months; some colleagues converted quickly and others required weeks of support. She contrasts sustained immersion with a two-day workshop or a six-week scoped pilot. Successful adoption is conditioned on applied practice, workflow redesign, accessible machine-readable context, human checking and orchestration, and support from experienced practitioners. Enterprise constraints make these conditions harder to establish. Her suggested capability-transfer and acquisition pathways remain exploratory, not settled forecasts.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are knowledge workers, AI-native startups, large corporations and government agencies, and software and consulting providers; the public is implicated through high-stakes organisational decisions.
pts.d: Individual workers must develop practical fluency, reorganise information and exercise judgement over agent actions and outputs. Small AI-native teams are portrayed as holding a capability advantage because they can experiment and redesign work, although Roberts's own team still needed intensive support. Large organisations face the greatest mismatch between need and ability to change, affecting employees who must learn new practices and leaders responsible for governance and implementation. Startups may become sources of transferable expertise or acquisition targets; software and consulting providers may combine deployment support with tooling. Roberts connects enterprise capability to decisions affecting millions but does not specify public-service outcomes. She makes no distinct claims about lawyers, law-firm staffing, legal fees, legal clients or access to justice.
